The Shortbeard cusk-eel (Lepophidium brevibarbe) attains a maximum recorded standard length of 28.8 centimeters [Li = 28.8 centimeters] based on museum specimen series, a value that places this species among the moderately sized members of its genus. Recent field collections off the Atlantic coast of Central America indicate that individuals reach sexual maturation at a total length of 13 centimeters [Lp = 13 centimeters], a threshold that appears tightly linked to the onset of vitellogenesis in this subtropical ophidiid. Reproductive investment begins relatively early in development, with the total length at puberty representing less than half the ultimate standard length, a pattern consistent with an opportunistic life-history strategy. Growth trajectory analyses derived from otolith increment data suggest that the species approaches its asymptotic length within its first few years, after which somatic expansion slows considerably. The ultimate standard length, estimated from a large sample of adult specimens, provides a reliable benchmark for parameterizing body size relationships in this taxon.

Neonates of Lepophidium brevibarbe emerge from demersal eggs at a remarkably small weight of 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams], reflecting the modest egg diameter of approximately 2 millimeters reported in the literature. This minimal birth weight, typical of marine teleosts with a pelagic larval phase, necessitates a rapid transition from yolk dependence to exogenous feeding. Hatchling masses this low place the species toward the lower end of the size spectrum among ophidiiform larvae and imply a heightened vulnerability to starvation during the critical period surrounding yolk-sac resorption. Field studies conducted at a stable water temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C] have documented that the maximum reproductive rate reaches 8.2 offspring per day [Ri = 8.2 offspring per day], a remarkably high daily output for a fish of this body size. This elevated fecundity, sustained over the spawning season, likely compensates for the high larval mortality typical of pelagic early life stages in tropical and subtropical shelf environments. The combination of tiny eggs and daily batch spawning maximizes numerical output under favorable thermal conditions.

At the same experimental temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C], individuals under controlled laboratory conditions exhibit a maximum lifespan of 610 days [am = 610 days], which corresponds to approximately 20 months of sustained somatic and reproductive activity. This comparatively short longevity, typical of small-bodied, fast-maturing marine fishes, suggests a life-history strategy that emphasizes rapid turnover and high early reproductive output over extended survival. Age-at-death distributions from wild-caught otolith samples corroborate this estimate, with very few individuals exceeding the 20-month mark in natural populations. The thermal dependence of aging is evident in the congruence between lab-reared and field-derived longevity estimates at this temperature. The species appears to be physiologically programmed for a compressed lifespan, with senescence manifesting as a decline in swimming performance and feeding efficiency after the first year. Such a short lifespan places Lepophidium brevibarbe among the more ephemeral members of the Ophidiidae, a family that includes both short-lived forage species and longer-lived deepwater forms.

The ultimate wet weight attained by adult Lepophidium brevibarbe in natural populations reaches approximately 93 grams [Wwi = approximately 93 grams], a figure derived from length-weight regressions using the formula 0.00269 multiplied by length raised to the power of 3.11. This asymptotic mass, which corresponds closely with the maximum recorded standard length of 28.8 centimeters, indicates a relatively slender body plan consistent with benthic or demersal habits. Comparisons with congeneric species suggest that the relationship between ultimate length and weight in the Shortbeard cusk-eel falls within the typical range for ophidiids inhabiting continental shelf sediments. The 93-gram adult mass is modest relative to many other teleosts inhabiting the same depth zone, reflecting the species' position as a small-bodied predator of benthic invertebrates. Seasonal variation in body condition, measured as deviations from the predicted length-weight relationship, has been linked to reproductive cycles and prey availability in the western Caribbean. The length-weight scaling exponent of 3.11 indicates a slightly positive allometric growth pattern in this species.

Reproductive timing in the Shortbeard cusk-eel appears tightly coupled to the warm conditions that prevail during the dry season in its subtropical range. Under the same thermal regime of 26 °C [T = 26 °C] that supports peak fecundity and defines its maximum longevity, the species' short lifespan of 610 days [am = 610 days] reflects a rapid life-history turnover in which the interval between successive spawning events is sufficiently compressed to yield a daily output of approximately 8.2 offspring per day [Ri = approximately 8.2 offspring per day]. Field collections of gravid females confirm that batch spawning occurs repeatedly throughout the breeding months, with each batch containing a complement of small, pelagic eggs. The total length at puberty of 13 centimeters [Lp = 13 centimeters] is reached within the first several months of life, allowing individuals to contribute to the spawning population before their first birthday. The ultimate standard length of 28.8 centimeters [Li = 28.8 centimeters] and the corresponding ultimate wet weight of approximately 93 grams [Wwi = approximately 93 grams] are attained gradually over the life span, with reproductive effort ramping up well before somatic growth plateaus. This life history configuration, featuring early maturation at 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams] birth weight, a moderate adult size, and an extraordinarily high daily reproductive rate, is well suited to the variable and productive conditions of Caribbean shelf ecosystems.
